title: Tomato, chocolate and coyote all come from the Aztecs’ language
body: Nahuatl was the language of the Mexica, the people we call the Aztecs, and under their empire it became a lingua franca for the merchants and elites of Mesoamerica. When the Spanish met its foods and animals they borrowed the names, and English borrowed them in turn: tomato from tōmatl, avocado from āhuacatl, coyote from coyōtl, plus chili, chipotle, chocolate, chayote, peyote and axolotl. Nahuatl is far from dead: about **1.7 million people** still speak it, most of them in central Mexico.

left.label: Aztec Empire
left.text: The tongue of the Mexica, and a lingua franca for traders and elites across Mesoamerica.

right.label: Today
right.text: About 1.7 million speakers, mostly in central Mexico, with smaller communities in the United States.

slides.heading: Which of Mexico’s indigenous languages has the most speakers?
slides.note: Speakers in Mexico at the 2020 census; Nahuatl’s 1.7 million is a rounded figure.
slides.explanation: Nahuatl leads with about 1.7 million speakers, ahead of Yucatec Maya, Tzeltal and Tzotzil.

slides.heading: Not just food
slides.text: Coyote comes from coyōtl. The axolotl salamander, the peyote cactus and the atlatl, a spear-thrower, all kept their Nahuatl names in English too.

slides.question: Which of these English words does not come from Nahuatl?
slides.explanation: Tomato (tōmatl), chocolate and avocado (āhuacatl) are Nahuatl loans. Potato reached English through Spanish from Caribbean and Andean languages, not from Nahuatl.
